docs.title: Welcome
docs.text: Nikita Bangiyev Datasheet as part of Fill-A-Bot for Team 201 Updated: October 25, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This is my individual datasheet for EGR 304. It shows my part of our team project, the parts I picked for my board, and how my board is powered.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
Fill-A-Bot is our team's automatic liquid dispenser. You pick how much liquid you want, press start, and it fills your cup and stops on its own. Each of us builds our own board, and the boards talk to each other over ribbon cables using plain digital wires (2 wires per signal, 4 states). Our full team report is on the Team 201 website.

  • Nikita Bangiyev: Main Control Board (me)
  • Cole Trask: flow sensing
  • Clay Belsher: pump control
  • Troy Reynolds: liquid amount sensing

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
I'm doing the Main Control Board. It reads the UP, DOWN, START, and STOP buttons, uses a photoresistor and an op amp to check that a cup is in place, sends simple 2-wire digital signals to my teammates' boards (pump command to Clay, preset to Troy) and reads theirs back (flow status from Cole, weight status from Troy), and shows the amount and status on a 16x2 LCD.

  • Block Diagram: how my board is laid out and connected
  • Component Selection: the parts I picked for my board and why
  • Schematics: the full schematic for my board
  • Power Budget: how much current my board needs and how it's powered

docs.title: Block Diagram
docs.text: Nikita Bangiyev, Team 201, Fill-A-Bot (automatic liquid dispenser)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I'm doing the main control board. The user picks one of 4 fill presets with the UP and DOWN buttons and presses START. My board tells Troy's board which preset was picked, tells Clay's board to run the pump, and then watches the flow status from Cole's board and the weight status from Troy's board. When Troy's board says the target is reached, my board stops the pump. If Cole's board says there's no flow, my board stops the pump and flashes the Fault LED. The amount and status show on a 16x2 LCD. My sensor is a photoresistor under the cup spot with an op amp and a low-pass filter, so the pump only starts when a cup is there.

The boards don't use UART, I2C, or SPI. Each signal between two boards is just 2 plain digital wires driven high or low, so it can send 4 states (00, 01, 10, 11). My board has 2 of these outputs (pump command and weight command) and 2 inputs (weight status and flow status).

Figure 1: Main control board block diagram (click to enlarge)

Source files: nikita-block-diagram-source.zip (draw.io file and PNG)

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
• 9V 2A regulated wall adapter (Triad WSU090-2000) into a barrel jack (Same Sky PJ-102AH)
  • T800mA fuse (Littelfuse 0218.800MXP) in a 5x20mm holder right after the jack
  • LM1086IT-5.0 linear regulator makes 5V (1.5A max, 4.9 to 5.1V) for the whole board
  • The regulator has a heat sink (Same Sky HSE14-384225P) with an insulating pad, because its tab is at 5V
  • The Nano gets 5V on VTG with VOFF tied to GND
  • D6 lights up when 9V is in, and D5 lights up when 5V is on
  • My power budget is 432mA with the 25% margin (see Power Budget)

docs.title: Pin Assignments
docs.text:
Pin Use Connects to RA0 Digital input SW1 UP button, next preset (active low, 10k pull-up) RA1 Digital input SW2 DOWN button, last preset RA2 Digital input SW3 START button, start the fill RA3 Digital input SW4 STOP button, cancel RF4 Digital input SW5 debug button RA5 ADC Cup sensor (op amp and low-pass filter output) RD0 Digital output D2 Dispensing LED (active low, 2.2k) RD1 Digital output D3 Done LED RD2 Digital output D4 Fault LED RF2 Digital output D1 debug LED RC0 Digital output LCD DB4 RC1 Digital output LCD DB5 RC2 Digital output LCD DB6 RC3 Digital output LCD DB7 RC4 Digital output LCD RS RC5 Digital output LCD E RC7 / RC6 Digital inputs Flow status S1 / S0, from Cole (J1 pins 3 / 4) RD4 / RD3 Digital outputs Pump command C1 / C0, to Clay (J2 pins 1 / 2) RF6 / RF5 Digital outputs Weight command C1 / C0, to Troy (J3 pins 1 / 2) RE1 / RE0 Digital inputs Weight status S1 / S0, from Troy (J3 pins 3 / 4)

All four inputs from the ribbons (RC7, RC6, RE1, RE0) have a 100k pull-down, so an unplugged cable reads 00.

docs.title: Ribbon Connectors
docs.text:
J1 goes to Cole, J2 to Clay, and J3 to Troy. All three use the same layout and follow the class standard (pins 1-5 digital, 6-7 analog, 8 ground). Pins 1-2 are always my outputs, pins 3-4 are always the teammate's outputs coming back to me, and pin 8 is ground.

Pin J1 (Cole) J2 (Clay) J3 (Troy) 1 Not connected Pump command C1 out (RD4) Weight command C1 out (RF6) 2 Not connected Pump command C0 out (RD3) Weight command C0 out (RF5) 3 Flow status S1 in (RC7) Not connected Weight status S1 in (RE1) 4 Flow status S0 in (RC6) Not connected Weight status S0 in (RE0) 5-7 Not connected Not connected Not connected 8 GND GND GND

There's no power pin on the ribbon. Every board has its own adapter and regulator, and pins 1-7 have to go to the microcontroller. All signals are 5V logic.

docs.title: Signal Codes
docs.text:
Bit 1 is the first pin of the pair and bit 0 is the second. 00 is the safe default on every signal.

Signal Direction 00 01 10 11 Pump command Me to Clay Stop Run Not used (stop) Not used (stop) Weight command Me to Troy Preset 1 Preset 2 Preset 3 Preset 4 Weight status Troy to me Not ready Below target (filling) Target reached Error Flow status Cole to me No flow Flowing Not used (no flow) Sensor fault

The team is still picking the four preset amounts. The weight command can sit at Preset 1 by default because it never turns anything on. Only the pump command does, and its default is Stop.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• I switched from a 4-digit 7-segment display to a 16x2 LCD, because the team requirements need words like Ready, Filling, and Finished. The LCD has its own controller, so the HT16K33 driver is gone. It was discontinued anyway.
  • The op amp is needed because a photoresistor and resistor alone don't count as an analog sensor. U3A buffers the divider and U3B amplifies it with a gain of -3 around a 2.5V reference. Then R10 and C9 make a low-pass filter (about 16 Hz) before the ADC.
  • The team ribbon used to be I2C, and then UART. On Oct 22 we dropped both (the professor suggested it), so now each signal is 2 plain digital wires with 4 states. It's simpler to wire, test with an LED or meter, and debug.
  • I switched from the LM7805 to the LM1086 because the LCD backlight needs 4.9 to 5.1V, and a 7805 can be 4.75 to 5.25V.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
My subsystem: Main Control Board. This is an individual assignment, so this page covers the blocks in my individual block diagram. Clay's pump, Cole's flow sensor, and Troy's load cell are on their own Component Selection pages. The parts I picked for my board are in bold.

My board reads the UP, DOWN, START, and STOP buttons, checks that a cup is there, sends and reads simple 2-wire digital signals on the ribbon cables to my teammates' boards, and shows the amount and status on a display. The assignment says not to make tables for the microcontroller, buttons, LEDs, resistors, or capacitors, so those don't have tables. Prices are from DigiKey for one part (October 2026).

docs.title: 1. Power Source
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Triad Magnetics WSU090-13009V 1.3A wall adapter$8.65/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive adapter- In stock at DigiKey- Long 6 ft cord - Fine for my real load, but less than the regulator's 1.5A rating- Output can be off by 5%- Big body blocks the next outlet Option 2.MEAN WELL GST18U09-P1J9V 2A wall adapter$14.10/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 2A is more than enough- Lowest ripple of the three- Wide temperature range - Most expensive adapter- Out of stock at DigiKey- Short 1.2 m cord Option 3.Triad Magnetics WSU090-20009V 2A wall adapter$12.43/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 2A covers the regulator's full 1.5A- In stock at DigiKey- Long 6 ft cord - Costs more than the 1.3A one- Output can be off by 5%- Only rated up to 40 C

Choice: Option 3: Triad WSU090-2000 (Main Control Board)

Rationale: The LM1086 regulator is rated for up to 1.5A, but that's only how much it can supply. It's not what my board actually uses. My board uses 345.8mA. With the 25% safety margin that's 432.3mA. The regulator uses about 10mA itself and the 9V power LED uses about 2mA, so the adapter has to give about 444mA. All three adapters can do that. The class power budget template also checks the adapter against the regulator's full 1.5A rating, so I picked a 2A adapter to pass that check too (2000mA - 1500mA = 500mA left). The Triad is in stock and costs less than the MEAN WELL, and it has the 5.5 x 2.1 mm center-positive plug. The full numbers are on my Power Budget page.

docs.title: 2. Barrel Jack
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Same Sky PJ-102AHDC barrel jack, 2.0 mm pin, through hole$0.77/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rated 5A, way more than my board needs- Inexpensive- Lots in stock at DigiKey - 2.0 mm pin, so I have to check how tight the 2.1 mm plug fits- Right-angle part has to sit at the board edge- Costs a little more than the PJ-102A Option 2.Same Sky PJ-102ADC barrel jack, 2.0 mm pin, through hole$0.70/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive jack- Same size and pins as the PJ-102AH- Lots in stock at DigiKey - Only rated 2.5A- Same 2.0 mm pin fit question- Less extra current room than the AH version Option 3.Switchcraft RAPC722XDC barrel jack, through hole$2.23/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rated 5A- Very common jack- Lots in stock at DigiKey - Most expensive jack, about 3x the others- Different footprint than the Same Sky jacks- No real advantage for my 0.44A load

Choice: Option 1: Same Sky PJ-102AH (Main Control Board)

Rationale: The course requires a barrel jack for the 9V adapter. The PJ-102AH is rated 5A, so it has a lot of room over my 0.44A. It's inexpensive and it's already in my block diagram. DigiKey lists its mating plug as 5.5 x 2.0 mm, and my adapter plug is 5.5 x 2.1 mm, so I'll check the fit when the parts come in.

docs.title: 3. 5V Linear Regulator
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Texas Instruments LM7805CT/NOPB5V 1.5A, TO-220$1.86/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Really common part- Built-in thermal protection- Easy to solder - Output can be 4.75 to 5.25V- About 2V dropout- Out of stock Option 2.STMicroelectronics L7805CV5V 1.5A, TO-220$1.08/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive regulator- Lots in stock- Standard 7805 pinout - Output can be 4.75 to 5.25V- About 2V dropout- Gets just as hot as the others Option 3.Texas Instruments LM1086IT-5.0/NOPB5V 1.5A low dropout, TO-220$2.58/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Output stays 4.9 to 5.1V- Only 1.5V max dropout- In stock at DigiKey - Needs an output cap with some ESR to stay stable (TI recommends 10uF tantalum or 50uF aluminum)- Different pinout than a 7805- Costs a little more

Choice: Option 3: TI LM1086IT-5.0/NOPB (Main Control Board)

Rationale: My LCD backlight needs 4.9 to 5.1V, and the LM1086 is the only one here that stays in that range. The 7805s can go up to 5.25V. I'll put a 10uF tantalum capacitor on the output, which is one of the two options TI recommends for stability.

docs.title: 4. Regulator Heat Sink
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Same Sky HSE14-384225PTO-220 heat sink$2.24/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - 10 C/W at 1W in still air- Small 41.6 x 25 mm footprint- In stock at DigiKey - 38.1 mm tall- Needs an insulating pad since the LM1086 tab is at 5V- Not as strong as the Boyd parts Option 2.Boyd 529802B02500GTO-220 heat sink$2.02/eachDigiKey / Catalog - Lower thermal resistance (3.7 C/W at a 75 C rise)- Most inexpensive heat sink- Same size footprint - Out of stock at DigiKey- Also 38.1 mm tall- More cooling than I need Option 3.Boyd 530002B02500GTO-220 heat sink$4.03/eachDigiKey / Catalog - Lowest thermal resistance (2.6 C/W at a 75 C rise)- In stock at DigiKey- Same size footprint - 63.5 mm tall, hard to fit in a box- Most expensive heat sink- Way more cooling than I need

Choice: Option 1: Same Sky HSE14-384225P (Main Control Board)

Rationale: It's in stock, small enough for my board, and enough to keep the regulator cool. The Boyd 529802B02500G is out of stock, and the taller Boyd is way bigger than I need. The Boyd numbers are at a 75 C rise, so they aren't measured the same way as the Same Sky number.

Here is how I checked the regulator temperature:

What Value Where it comes from Highest adapter voltage 9.45V 9V + 5% (Triad datasheet) Lowest regulator output 4.9V LM1086 datasheet Output current 432.3mA My power budget, with the 25% margin Regulator's own current 10mA max LM1086 datasheet Heat = (9.45 - 4.9) x 0.4323 + 9.45 x 0.010 2.06W Calculated Junction to case 4.0 C/W LM1086 datasheet (TO-220, output section) Insulating pad 1.0 C/W My guess (a Bergquist SP900S pad is listed at 0.61 C/W) Heat sink 10 C/W HSE14-384225P datasheet (still air, 1W) Air inside the enclosure 40 C My assumption Junction temp = 40 + 2.06 x (4.0 + 1.0 + 10) about 71 C Calculated Limit 125 C LM1086 datasheet (control section)

So it should stay well under the limit. The heat sink datasheet shows 19.2 C of rise at 2W (9.6 C/W), so using 10 C/W is a little on the safe side. I'll still check the real temperature once the board is built.

docs.title: 5. Cup Sensor (Analog)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103Photoresistor (LDR)$0.72/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Big change between light and shadow- Sees normal room light- Used it in my photoresistor lab - Slow (about 60ms)- Room light changes the reading- Each one is a little different Option 2.Vishay TEPT4400Phototransistor$0.50/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive sensor- Reacts quickly to changes- Responds like the human eye - Big part-to-part difference- Can max out in bright light- Narrow viewing angle Option 3.Vishay BPW34Photodiode$1.37/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Output is very linear with light- Large sensing area- Reacts very quickly - Needs a different amp circuit- Also picks up infrared- Really small currents

Choice: Option 1: Advanced Photonix PDV-P8103 (Main Control Board)

Rationale: It's simple, inexpensive, and I already know how it works from lab. It sits under the cup spot with a 10k resistor, and a cup's shadow drops the voltage. A divider alone doesn't count as an analog sensor for this class, so it goes through the op amp below before the ADC. I'll still need to test it with our real cups, since a clear cup may not make much of a shadow.

docs.title: 6. Op Amp
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Microchip MCP6002-I/PDual op amp, 8-pin DIP$0.45/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rail-to-rail on 5V- Two op amps in one chip- Very low current - Higher offset voltage- Only 1MHz bandwidth- Doesn't quite reach the rails Option 2.Texas Instruments TLV2372IPDual op amp, 8-pin DIP$2.38/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Rail-to-rail input and output- Wide supply range- 3MHz bandwidth - About 5x the price- Uses more current- Speed isn't needed Option 3.Texas Instruments OPA2340UADual op amp, SOIC-8$4.63/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Lowest offset voltage- 5.5MHz bandwidth- Rail-to-rail on 5V - Most expensive op amp here- Surface mount is harder to solder- Uses the most current

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6002-I/P (Main Control Board)

Rationale: A cup sensor is slow, so I don't need a fast op amp. The MCP6002 is inexpensive, comes in a DIP, and has two op amps. One buffers the LDR, and the other amplifies it with a gain of -3 around a 2.5V reference (Rin 10k, Rf 30k). I'll set the cup threshold in code after testing.

docs.title: 7. Display
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Lucky Light KW4-56NCUYA-P (Adafruit 811)4-digit 7-segment display$3.95/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Big, easy to read digits- Bright in any lighting- Inexpensive for 4 digits - Can't show words like Ready or Filling- Can't show units- Needs a driver chip Option 2.Kingbright PDC54-11SURKWA2-character 14-segment display$5.60/each (need 4)DigiKey / Datasheet - Can show letters- Bright, high contrast- Big 0.53 in characters - 4 of them are too wide for my board- Needs a driver chip- Only 8 characters Option 3.Newhaven Display NHD-0216K1Z-FL-YBW16x2 character LCD$7.83/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Shows the amount, units, and status at once- Built-in controller, no driver chip- Backlight makes it easy to read - Backlight uses up to 156mA- Needs a contrast pot- Uses 6 pins

Choice: Option 3: Newhaven NHD-0216K1Z-FL-YBW (Main Control Board)

Rationale: Our team requirements say the display has to show the amount, the units, and words like Ready, Filling, and Finished. The LCD is the only option that can do all of that at once. It wires straight to the Nano in 4-bit mode (RC0-RC5), so I don't need a driver chip or a serial backpack board.

docs.title: 8. Ribbon Cable Header
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Wurth Elektronik 612008216212x4 box header, 2.54 mm$1.03/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Most inexpensive header- Keying slot so the ribbon only goes in one way- Gold-plated contacts - No latch to lock the cable in- Shorter shroud than the 3M part- I need three of them (J1-J3) Option 2.3M N2508-6002-RB2x4 box header, 2.54 mm$2.31/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Keyed so the cable only fits one way- Rated 5A per contact- Wide -55 to 105 C range - Most expensive header, about 2x the others- Fewer in stock- No latch to lock the cable in Option 3.Amphenol ICC 75869-132LF2x4 box header, 2.54 mm$1.10/eachDigiKey / Datasheet - Almost as inexpensive as the Wurth- Keyed so the cable only fits one way- Lots in stock at DigiKey - No latch to lock the cable in- Costs a little more than the Wurth- Datasheet link is from a distributor, not Amphenol

Choice: Option 1: Wurth Elektronik 61200821621 (Main Control Board)

Rationale: The class uses an 8-wire ribbon cable with a 2x4 connector between boards, and I need three (J1 to Cole, J2 to Clay, J3 to Troy). The Wurth is the least expensive, it's keyed so the cable can't go in backwards, and it's the part already in my block diagram.

docs.title: Pin Assignments
docs.text:
This is how I'll set up each pin in MCC (Pin Grid View). "Start high" means the pin's LAT bit is set to 1 at power-up. None of the pins use the internal weak pull-ups, because every input already has an outside pull-up or pull-down on my board.

Pin Subsystem MCC setting Connects to RA0 Buttons Digital input SW1 UP button (next preset), 10k pull-up, active low RA1 Buttons Digital input SW2 DOWN button (last preset), 10k pull-up, active low RA2 Buttons Digital input SW3 START button, 10k pull-up, active low RA3 Buttons Digital input SW4 STOP button (cancel), 10k pull-up, active low RF4 Debug Digital input SW5 debug button, 10k pull-up, active low RA5 Cup sensor Analog input (ADC channel ANA5) Op amp and low-pass filter output RD0 Status LEDs Digital output, start high D2 Dispensing LED (yellow), 2.2k, active low RD1 Status LEDs Digital output, start high D3 Done LED (green), 2.2k, active low RD2 Status LEDs Digital output, start high D4 Fault LED (red), 2.2k, active low RF2 Debug Digital output, start high D1 debug LED (red), 2.2k, active low RC0 LCD Digital output, start low LCD DB4 RC1 LCD Digital output, start low LCD DB5 RC2 LCD Digital output, start low LCD DB6 RC3 LCD Digital output, start low LCD DB7 RC4 LCD Digital output, start low LCD RS RC5 LCD Digital output, start low LCD E (100k pull-down R24) RC7 Flow status from Cole Digital input J1 pin 3 (S1), 100k pull-down RC6 Flow status from Cole Digital input J1 pin 4 (S0), 100k pull-down RD4 Pump command to Clay Digital output, start low J2 pin 1 (C1) RD3 Pump command to Clay Digital output, start low J2 pin 2 (C0) RF6 Weight command to Troy Digital output, start low J3 pin 1 (C1) RF5 Weight command to Troy Digital output, start low J3 pin 2 (C0) RE1 Weight status from Troy Digital input J3 pin 3 (S1), 100k pull-down RE0 Weight status from Troy Digital input J3 pin 4 (S0), 100k pull-down VTG Power 5V from the LM1086 (VOFF tied to GND) GND Ground Board ground and J1-J3 pin 8

The ribbon signals don't use UART, I2C, or SPI. Each one is 2 plain digital pins, so it has 4 states (00, 01, 10, 11), and 00 is the safe default. The ribbon outputs start low so the pump command is 00 (stop) at power-up, and the 100k pull-downs make an unplugged cable read 00. The codes for each signal are on my Block Diagram page. Ribbon pins 5-7 aren't connected on my board, and there's no power on the ribbon since every board has its own regulator. The spare Nano pins go to the J5 and J6 extra headers.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• TP1-TP17 are bare test pads on the PCB, so they don't need a part.
  • JP1-JP11 are 2-pin headers with a jumper shunt on each, so the shunts are their own line.
  • The LCD plugs into J7, a 16-pin socket, so the LCD gets a 16-pin male header soldered on.
  • The screw, nut, and shoulder washer that hold U2 on its heat sink aren't picked yet.
  • How the Nano attaches to the PCB (sockets or soldered headers) gets picked with the PCB layout.
  • The ribbon cables between boards are shared by the team, so they aren't on my BOM.
  • The Omron B3F switch line is now sold under the Aratas name on DigiKey. The part number didn't change.

docs.title: Schematics
docs.text:
This is the schematic for my Main Control Board (rev 3, October 25, 2026). It has the 9-12V power input and 5V regulator, the Curiosity Nano, the cup sensor with the op amp, the LCD, the buttons and LEDs, and the three ribbon cables to my teammates' boards. Each signal on the ribbons is 2 plain digital wires with 4 states (00, 01, 10, 11). There's no UART, I2C, or SPI between boards.

Figure 1: Main Control Board schematic (click to enlarge)

docs.title: How It Meets the Requirements
docs.text:
The numbers in brackets are from our team's Product Requirements page ("Design" means the Requirement Criteria Specifications list).

  • Power [6.7]: The barrel jack takes 9-12V, goes through a swappable T800mA fuse, and the LM1086 linear regulator makes 5V. It has the input and output caps from the TI datasheet (10uF tantalum on the output) and a 0.1uF bypass cap at every IC power pin. The worst-case load is 432mA with margin, well under the regulator's 1.5A, and the heat sink keeps it near 71 C. D6 and D5 show that the 9V and 5V rails are on.
  • Picking the amount [2.1, 3.1, 4.1, Design 2.4]: UP and DOWN pick one of the 4 fill presets, and START starts the fill. Each button has a 10k pull-up and an RC debounce, so one press reads as one press. J9 lets the buttons be mounted off the board.
  • Stopping at any time [6.1, Design 1.5, Design 3.4]: STOP is its own button on RA3. The firmware sets the pump command to 00 (stop) from any step.
  • Cup sensor: The photoresistor goes through a buffer, a gain stage, and a low-pass filter into the ADC (RA5), so the pump only starts when a cup is in place. This answers the open question on our requirements page about checking for a container before dispensing.
  • Display and status [3.2, 3.3, 3.4, Design 2.1]: The 16x2 LCD shows the preset amount and the status (Ready, Filling, Finished, Error). Three LEDs show Dispensing, Done, and Fault, and the Fault LED flashes when there's no flow.
  • Measuring and stopping at the target [1.2, 2.2, 2.3, 6.4]: My board sends the preset to Troy's board (RF6, RF5) and the run command to Clay's board (RD4, RD3). It watches the weight status from Troy (RE1, RE0) and the flow status from Cole (RC7, RC6), and stops the pump when the target is reached. J1, J2, and J3 follow the class ribbon standard with pin 8 as ground and no power pin. Pins 1-2 are always my outputs and pins 3-4 are always the teammate's outputs back to me.
  • No unintended dispensing [2.6]: The ribbon outputs start low, so the pump command is 00 (stop) at power-up. R26-R29 are 100k pull-downs on my four ribbon inputs, so an unplugged cable reads 00 (no flow or not ready) instead of floating, and the pump won't run.
  • Repeat fills [2.4]: After a fill is done, the firmware goes back to picking a preset without a restart.
  • Debugging: There's a debug LED (RF2), a debug button (RF4), jumpers to cut the power and every ribbon signal, 17 test points (including one on every ribbon signal), and spare Nano pins on the J5 and J6 headers.
  • Part numbers and ERC: Every part has its manufacturer part number in the KiCad file, matching my BOM. ERC shows 0 errors and 0 warnings (the report is in the KiCad ZIP).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This power budget checks that my 9V adapter and 5V regulator can run everything on my Main Control Board at the same time, with a 25% safety margin. It only covers my board, since each teammate has their own adapter and regulator. I used the class power budget template. Everything runs off one 5V rail except the 9V power LED (D6), which sits before the regulator.

My real draw from the adapter is 444.299mA (432.268mA, plus 10mA for the regulator itself, plus 2.031mA for the 9V power LED), so there's a lot of room left.

docs.text: N/A. My board runs off a wall adapter.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The 2A adapter and the LM1086 can easily power everything on my board with the 25% margin, and nothing comes out negative. The biggest load is the LCD backlight. The regulator turns about 2W into heat, so it gets a heat sink, which keeps it around 71 C (its limit is 125 C).

Microchip only lists the PIC's max current at 3V, not 5V, so I used a safe upper estimate of 170mA for the Nano. The real number should be a lot lower, and I'll measure the actual board current once it's built.

docs.title: Ribbon Wiring for All Four Boards
docs.text:
On Oct 22 our team dropped UART and I2C between boards. Each signal is now 2 plain digital wires (4 states), and 00 is the safe default. The ribbon cable is straight through, so pin 1 on my header is pin 1 on the teammate's header. This is what each board has to wire to match my board.

Ribbon pin Cole (flow, J1) Clay (pump, J2) Troy (weight, J3) 1 Not used Pump command C1 in (from my RD4) Weight command C1 in (from my RF6) 2 Not used Pump command C0 in (from my RD3) Weight command C0 in (from my RF5) 3 Flow status S1 out (to my RC7) Not used Weight status S1 out (to my RE1) 4 Flow status S0 out (to my RC6) Not used Weight status S0 out (to my RE0) 5-7 Not used Not used Not used 8 GND GND GND
  • All boards use 5V logic.
  • Every input gets a 100k pull-down, so an unplugged cable reads 00.
  • Every output starts low (00) at power-up.
  • There's no power pin on the ribbon.

docs.title: Main Board States
docs.text:
This is the plan for my board's firmware, based on Cole's software flow chart. It's a draft and the timing numbers will be tuned on the real boards.

State Pump command Weight command What it's waiting for Goes to Idle / select preset 00 (stop) Preset 1-4 UP / DOWN change the preset. START with a cup in place and weight status 01 Filling Filling 01 (run) Preset (locked) Weight status 10 Done No flow (flow status not 01) for 3 seconds, or flow status 11 Error STOP pressed, or the cup is removed Cancel Error (no flow) 00 (stop) Preset Fault LED flashes until STOP is pressed Idle Done / reset 00 (stop) Preset Shows Finished for 3 seconds Idle Cancel 00 (stop) Preset Shows Canceled for 1 second Idle

STOP cancels from any state. A weight status of 11 (error) also goes to the error state, with a different message on the LCD. The ribbon inputs only count once they read the same 3 times in a row (10 ms apart), so a read in the middle of a change gets ignored. The container weight is hard-coded on Troy's board for the demo.
